candidates.attacker_control: SAML paths: the caller fully controls the compressed bytes — `SAMLResponse` (redirect binding, `isSupportDeflateEncoding()` defaults true, AbstractRequestAssertionConsumerHandler.java:67,282-283) or the Base64 assertion/token consumed by AbstractSamlBase64InHandler.handleToken (`useDeflateEncoding = true` by default, line 32/50-51), including form-field/body-sized values; inflation runs before signature/issuer/condition validation. JOSE path: the protected header `zip: DEF` and the ciphertext are attacker-supplied; anyone able to produce a validly encrypted JWE (public-key key management such as RSA-OAEP/ECDH-ES with the recipient's public key) controls the plaintext and can make it a DEFLATE bomb. A DEFLATE stream can amplify ~1000:1, so a modest request can force gigabytes of heap allocation.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked for an existing cap: CompressionUtils has no max-size overload; JoseConstants/KeyProperties have no decompression-limit property (only RSSEC_DECRYPTION_MAX_PBES2_COUNT, i.e., the earlier p2c DoS fix is present at rt/rs/security/jose-parent/jose/.../PbesHmacAesWrapKeyDecryptionAlgorithm.java:67-69, showing the maintainers cap one JOSE DoS but not this one); IOUtils.readBytesFromStream is unbounded. Checked that the SAML XML parsing after inflation is otherwise hardened (StaxUtils disables DTD/external entities), and that the XOP URL-follow SSRF fixes (core/aegis `org.apache.cxf.attachment.xop.follow.urls`, default false) are present, so those neighbouring CVEs are not the issue. For the JWE path, AES-GCM/CBC-HMAC tag validation precedes inflation (AesCbcHmacJweDecryption validates the tag in doDecrypt before super.doDecrypt), which is stated as a precondition rather than glossed over. No code path was found that bounds the inflated output or rejects over-compressed input.
candidates.impact: Remote denial of service: unbounded heap allocation and CPU burn on a server thread, leading to OutOfMemoryError/GC death of the JVM or eviction of tenant workloads. Because the SAML inflation occurs before any signature/issuer/audience validation, an unauthenticated client can trigger it repeatedly (per-request allocation ~1000x the submitted payload). No confidentiality/integrity impact; no evidence of RCE.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses one of the affected features: CXF SAML SSO (RequestAssertionConsumerFilter / RACS with redirect binding and default deflate support), the JAX-RS SAML assertion handlers (useDeflateEncoding default true), or JWE decryption with a key the attacker can encrypt to. No special misconfiguration or elevated privilege is required for the SAML pre-validation paths (unauthenticated); the JWE path requires the ability to build a valid JWE (the content is authenticated before inflation for AES-GCM and AES-CBC-HMAC). Default request-size limits of the surrounding container are the only brake.
candidates.root_cause: CompressionUtils.inflate(byte[], boolean) (core/src/main/java/org/apache/cxf/common/util/CompressionUtils.java:36-57) loops `while (!inflater.finished())` writing every produced chunk into an unbounded ByteArrayOutputStream, with no maximum-output-size parameter or check, and no caller-supplied cap. Every reachable caller passes raw, caller/attacker-influenced bytes: AbstractSamlBase64InHandler.handleToken inflates a Base64 `assertion` **before** validateToken()/signature verification (rt/rs/security/xml/.../AbstractSamlBase64InHandler.java:32,41-53); AbstractRequestAssertionConsumerHandler.readSAMLResponse inflates the redirect-binding `SAMLResponse` **before** any response/assertion validation (rt/rs/security/sso/saml/.../AbstractRequestAssertionConsumerHandler.java:279-288, reached from the @PreMatching RequestAssertionConsumerFilter for an unauthenticated GET, lines 44-74); and for JOSE the JWE `zip` protected header alone sets compressionSupported (rt/rs/security/jose-parent/jose/.../AbstractJweDecryption.java:60-72) so CryptoUtils.processBytes inflates after `Cipher.doFinal` (rt/security/.../crypto/CryptoUtils.java:542-580, esp. 578-580). No MAX/decompression size property exists in JoseConstants or KeyProperties (searched `MAX`, `maxDeflat`, `MAX_DEFLAT`, `decompression`: only the p2c limit exists), and IOUtils.readBytesFromStream is also unbounded (core/.../helpers/IOUtils.java:430-440).
candidates.title: Decompression bomb: unbounded DEFLATE inflation of attacker-supplied payloads in CompressionUtils.inflate (SAML assertion/SSO handlers and JWE zip=DEF)
candidates.trace: GET /…?SAMLResponse=<base64(deflate-bomb)> → RequestAssertionConsumerFilter.filter (prematching, no auth) → doProcessSamlResponse → createSecurityContext → readSAMLResponse(postBinding=false) → Base64Utility.decode → new DeflateEncoderDecoder().inflateToken(...) (rt/rs/security/xml/.../DeflateEncoderDecoder.java:31-34) → CompressionUtils.inflate → bounded-size input, unbounded `inflatedToken` growth → OOM/GC thrash before validateSamlResponseProtocol/validateSamlSSOResponse run. Equivalent pre-validation path: AbstractSamlBase64InHandler.handleToken → inflateToken → validateToken. JOSE variant: JWE with protected header {`zip`:`DEF`} → JweCompactConsumer/AbstractJweDecryption.doDecrypt (compressionSupported set purely from the header) → CryptoUtils.decryptBytes → processBytes → CompressionUtils.inflate(result, true) → unbounded expansion of the decrypted plaintext.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no build, tests, or payloads were executed, and the index provides no data/control-flow proof. I could not verify from the source whether the upstream fix for this snapshot targeted this shared sink (CompressionUtils) or only the JOSE wrapper, nor whether the benchmark's ground-truth issue is this one rather than another lead; the concrete container URL-length limit for the redirect-binding GET path and the app's request-size limits were not measured, and the exact heap needed to OOM a given deployment is unknown.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-409 Improper Handling of Highly Compressed Data (Data Amplification) / CWE-400 Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (DoS)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 5171 files, no symlinks/sensitive-name exclusions, no files >5 MiB; binary-like files are refused/skipped by the tools. Relation index scope: 5124 of 5171 files indexed (47 source files absent), 4150 Java files detected but only 928 parsed, 5 parse errors, 53721 symbols/120062 edges/156026 call sites, 106245 unresolved calls; control-flow and data-flow analyses are explicitly not implemented, Spring annotation edges are name-based only, and no build or tests were run. I accounted for those filters and did not treat index labels as verdicts. Inspected broadly by module: core (stax, attachment incl. AttachmentUtil/AttachmentDeserializer/AttachmentSerializer, uri/resource resolution, ws/addressing EndpointReferenceUtils, common/utils incl. CompressionUtils, bus/spring loading); rt/frontend (jaxrs providers/impl incl. RequestPreprocessor, XSLTJaxbProvider, jaxws handlers); rt/rs (search/SQLPrinterVisitor, extensions, description-swagger-ui/OpenAPI features, security cors/http-signature/jose/oauth2/saml-xml/sso-saml, SSE); rt/ws (security/WSS4J integration, trust/AbstractSTSClient, rm, transfer); rt/transports (servlet service-list, http/https/SSLUtils, netty/undertow/websocket entry points); services/sts; plus pom/release-notes and workflow files for dating the snapshot (~July 2024, 3.5.9 development cycle). Uninspected or only sampled: tools/* code generators, maven-plugins, most of systests/ and distribution samples, large parts of rt/bindings/corba, most JOSE/oauth2/SAML validation internals, and the ~47 files missing from the index.
limitations: Static review only: no code execution, no tests, no scanners, no exploit payloads, and no runtime confirmation of any finding; the candidate is a lead, not a proven vulnerability.

The P1 index has no control-flow, no data-flow, no semantic resolution, 106k unresolved calls and only 928/4150 Java files parsed; reachability and taint reasoning were therefore done by manual source reading and not exhaustively verified.

I could not compare this snapshot against the corresponding fixed upstream revision, so I cannot confirm which change(s) constitute the intended patch; the candidate describes a weakness that is demonstrably present in the snapshot rather than a verified ground-truth match.

The JWE branch of the candidate needs the ability to construct a validly encrypted token (public-key key management) because AEAD tag validation precedes inflation; the SAML branches are pre-validation but the redirect-binding GET path is constrained by container URL length. Actual impact depends on deployment heap and request-size limits that were not measured.

Coverage is partial: tools/*, maven-plugins, most systests and samples, CORBA bindings and large parts of the JOSE/OAuth2/SAML validation code were only sampled, and 47 source files are absent from the relation index.

rejected_leads.lead: Path traversal in Swagger UI resource serving: SwaggerUiResourceLocator.locate (rt/rs/description-swagger-ui/.../SwaggerUiResourceLocator.java:45-61) concatenates the request-controlled `resourcePath` into the root URL without rejecting `..`, and it is reachable via SwaggerUiService.getResource (@Path("api-docs") + @Path("{resource:.*}"), lines 78-86) and SwaggerUiResourceFilter (lines 49-56, which also calls exists()→openConnection().connect() on the derived URL).
rejected_leads.reason: I could not establish a reliable attacker-controlled traversal: SwaggerUiResolver.checkUiRoot only returns `jar:`-prefixed roots (lines 59-72), where `..` entry lookups generally fail; only an OSGi/exploded (file:) root would make it exploitable, and the URI is also subject to container normalization. Kept as an unconfirmed lead, not the submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SSRF / local file read in WS-Trust client metadata handling: AbstractSTSClient.configureViaEPR dereferences the `MetadataSection/@Location` from a remote WS-MEX response through downloadSchema() → DocumentBuilder.parse(schemaLocation) (rt/ws/security/.../AbstractSTSClient.java:543-547, 615-623), which accepts file:/http: URLs.
rejected_leads.reason: Dereferencing the MEX Location is the protocol's intended behaviour, the code is client-side and only reached via configureViaEPR (STS/EPR configuration), and the XML parser is already XXE-hardened; attacker control over the remote MEX response is indirect, so I did not treat it as the strongest evidence-backed candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: XSLTJaxbProvider sets FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING but not XMLConstants.ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/ACCESS_EXTERNAL_STYLESHEET (unlike WadlGenerator.java:1310-1317), and createTemplatesFromContext() loads a template from the `xslt.template` message property (provide/XSLTJaxbProvider.java:504-537).
rejected_leads.reason: Stylesheet/template locations are application/annotation supplied, not request-controlled, and secure processing defaults to true; no attacker-controlled path to a malicious stylesheet was found, so this is a hardening gap rather than a demonstrated vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Other attacker-input-to-sink surfaces reviewed and found already protected: XOP/MTOM URL following (core/aegis followUrls default false), JOSE PBES2 iteration cap, WADL/XSLT TransformerFactory external-access restrictions, service-list HTML escaping/CSS-injection stripping, FIQL SQL visitor single-quote duplication, OAuth redirect_uri exact-match validation, CORS origin allow-list matching, and XML parsing XXE hardening.
rejected_leads.reason: No missing check or bypass could be demonstrated in these paths from source evidence; they are documented as checked counterevidence, not findings.

summary: Apache CXF 3.5.9-dev snapshot (5171 files; JAX-WS/JAX-RS framework). I reviewed request-handling and security-critical modules (core stax/attachment/uri, jaxrs frontend, transports, jose/oauth2/saml/xml security, ws/security, rs/extensions/search, description-swagger-ui, services/sts) with attention to attacker-controlled input reaching dangerous sinks (URL fetch, path handling, decompression, reflection, XSLT, SQL, CORS/origin checks). Most classic CXF hardening is present (StaxUtils/DOMUtils/TunedDocumentLoader XXE hardening, XOP `follow.urls` default-false in core + Aegis, JOSE PBES2 `p2c` cap, `StringEscapeUtils` escaping and CSS-injection stripping in the service-list page, `duplicateSingleQuoteIfNeeded` SQL escaping, OAuth redirect_uri exact matching). The single most concrete unfixed weakness I could trace end-to-end is unbounded DEFLATE decompression of attacker-supplied, highly-compressed data in the shared `CompressionUtils.inflate`, reached pre-validation from the SAML handlers (default `useDeflateEncoding=true`) and from JWE `zip: DEF` decryption; no size cap exists anywhere in the path and the analogous JOSE DoS (p2c) already got a cap, which is why this looks like an unfixed member of the same class. Candidate status is a lead only; I did not execute code and cannot confirm exploitability at runtime.
